title: Defence of Seneca and Plutarch
paragraphs: The familiarity I have with these two authors, and the help they have given to my age and to my book — which is, after all, wholly compiled out of what I have borrowed from them — obliges me to stand up for their honour.

As to Seneca: among the millions of little pamphlets that people of the so-called reformed religion scatter abroad in defence of their cause (some of them coming from so good a hand that it is a pity his pen is not employed on a better subject), I once saw one which, trying to construct a parallel between the government of our late poor King Charles IX and that of Nero, compared the late Cardinal of Lorraine with Seneca. Their fortunes were said to be alike in that both had been prime ministers to their princes, and their manners, characters, and conduct were said to be very nearly the same. In my opinion, this does the Cardinal a very great honour. I am one of those who have a high esteem for his wit, his eloquence, his zeal for religion and the service of his king, and his good fortune in having lived in an age when it was so unusual, so rare, and so necessary for the public good to have a churchman of high birth and dignity who was equal to his office. But to be honest, I do not think his ability comes within many degrees of Seneca's, nor was his virtue as clean, complete, or steady.

Now the book I am speaking of, to advance its case, gives a very damaging description of Seneca, borrowing its approach from Dion the historian — whose testimony I do not trust at all. Dion is inconsistent: after calling Seneca at one moment very wise and a mortal enemy to Nero's vices, he elsewhere makes him out to be greedy, a usurer, ambitious, soft, sensual, and a fraud as a philosopher. Yet Seneca's virtue shows up so lively and vigorously in his own writings, and he answers the charges so clearly — the riches, the lavish way of life — that I cannot believe any testimony against it. And besides, in matters of this sort it is much more reasonable to trust Roman historians than Greeks and foreigners. Tacitus and the rest speak honourably of both his life and his death, and present him as a thoroughly excellent and virtuous man. I will allege only one further reproach against Dion's report, and I cannot pass it over: his judgment of Roman affairs is so weak that he dares to defend Julius Caesar's cause against Pompey, and Antony's against Cicero.

Now to Plutarch. Jean Bodin is a good author of our times, with much sounder judgment than the crowd of scribblers of his age, and deserves to be read and considered. I find him, though, a little bold in a passage of his Method of History, where he accuses Plutarch not only of ignorance (which I would have let pass — that is beyond my judgment) but of "often writing things incredible and absolutely fabulous." Those are his own words. If he had merely said Plutarch reports things otherwise than they really were, that would be no great reproach: what we have not seen we have to take from other hands and on trust. I myself notice that Plutarch sometimes deliberately tells the same story two different ways — Hannibal's judgment of the three greatest captains there ever were, for example, goes one way in the Life of Flamininus and another in the Life of Pyrrhus. But to charge him with having taken impossible and incredible things as ready money is to accuse the most judicious author in the world of lacking judgment. And here is Bodin's example: "as when," he says, "Plutarch relates that a Spartan boy let his guts be torn out by a fox-cub he had stolen and hidden under his cloak, rather than let his theft be discovered." To begin with, I find the example badly chosen, because it is very hard to put a limit on what the soul's faculties can endure, whereas we have better grounds for knowing the limits of the body's strength. If I had been him, I would have picked an example of the second kind, and there are some less credible — among others Plutarch's tale of Pyrrhus, who, wounded as he was, struck one of his enemies, fully armed from head to foot, such a blow with his sword that he split him from crown to seat, so that the body fell apart in two pieces. In that example I find no great miracle, and I do not accept the excuse Plutarch makes by adding "as it is said," to suspend our belief. Unless it is in things received on authority, out of reverence for antiquity or religion, he would never have admitted, or asked us to believe, things incredible in themselves; and that the words "as it is said" are not really doing that work here is easy to see, because elsewhere on the same theme — the patience of Spartan children — he gives examples from his own time more unlikely than the fox-cub story. Cicero before him gave the same testimony, having (as he says) been on the spot: that even in their day there were children who, in the trial of patience they underwent at the altar of Diana, let themselves be whipped till the blood streamed down their bodies — not only without crying out, but without so much as a groan, and some until they voluntarily lost their lives. Plutarch, among a hundred other witnesses, also reports that at a sacrifice a live coal fell into the sleeve of a Spartan boy who was burning incense; he let his whole arm be roasted until the smell of his flesh reached those around him. By their custom there was nothing for which their reputation was more at stake, and for which they would suffer more blame and disgrace, than being caught in theft. I am so fully convinced of the greatness of those people that this story does not seem to me, as it does to Bodin, incredible — I do not even find it rare or strange. Spartan history is full of a thousand crueller and rarer examples; on this subject it is one long miracle.

Marcellinus, on the subject of theft, reports that in his day no kind of torture could compel the Egyptians, when caught in the act (and they were a people much given to it), so much as to give their names.

A Spanish peasant, racked for the names of the accomplices in the murder of the praetor Lucius Piso, shouted out at the height of the torment that his friends should not desert him but watch in full confidence — that no pain had the power to force one word of confession from him. That was all they got out of him the first day. The next day, as they were leading him to a second session on the rack, he wrenched himself out of his guards' hands and ran his head violently against a wall, beating his own brains out.

Epicharis, having tired out and glutted the cruelty of Nero's torturers — having endured their fire, their beating, their racks for a whole day without one syllable of confession about the conspiracy — was brought back to the rack the next day with her limbs almost torn to pieces. She slipped the ribbon of her robe through a running noose over one of the arms of her chair, suddenly thrust her head into it, and with the weight of her own body hanged herself. Having the courage to die in that manner — is it not fair to assume that she had deliberately given up her life to the trial of her resolve the day before, to mock the tyrant and encourage others to a similar attempt?

And anyone who will ask our troopers what they have seen in our civil wars will find examples of patience and stubborn resolution in this miserable age of ours, and among a rabble even softer than the Egyptians, that are worthy to be compared with what we have just related of Spartan virtue.

I know there have been simple peasants among us who have let the soles of their feet be grilled on a gridiron, their fingertips crushed with the cock of a pistol, and their bleeding eyes squeezed out of their heads by a cord twisted around their brows, before they would so much as agree to a ransom. I once saw a man left stark naked for dead in a ditch, his neck black and swollen, with the rope still around it that they had used to drag him all night at a horse's tail, his body wounded in a hundred places by daggers — not stabbed to kill him, but to torment and terrify him. He had endured it all, even to being beyond speech and feeling, resolved (as he told me himself) to die a thousand deaths rather than promise anything — and he had effectively borne one already in pain. He was, on top of that, one of the richest farmers in the country. How many have been seen patiently letting themselves be burnt and roasted for opinions taken on trust from others, and which they themselves did not understand? I have known a hundred women — and Gascony has a certain prerogative for obstinacy — whom you could sooner have made eat fire than give up an opinion they had taken hold of in anger. They only grow more exasperated under blows and constraint. And whoever invented the story of the woman who, in spite of every correction, threat, and beating, kept calling her husband a lousy knave, and who, when ducked over her head in water, lifted her hands above her head and made the sign of cracking lice — that storyteller was inventing a tale whose living image we see every day in the obstinacy of women. And obstinacy is the sister of constancy, at least in toughness and staying power.

We are not to judge what is possible and what is not by what is credible or incredible to our own understanding. As I have said elsewhere, it is a great fault — and yet one most men are guilty of, and I do not raise it now to point at Bodin — to refuse to believe of someone else what we ourselves could not or would not do. Everyone thinks the sovereign stamp of human nature is impressed in himself, and that all others must take their measure from it, so that any conduct that is not like his own must be faked or false. Is some action or capacity of another's put before such a man? The first thing he calls into consultation is his own example: as matters go with him, they must go with the rest of the world. A dangerous and intolerable folly. For my part, I consider some men, especially among the ancients, infinitely beyond me; and though I see clearly that I cannot come within a thousand paces of them, I still keep them in sight and judge what raises them so high, because I sense some seeds of it in myself — just as I do of the extreme meanness of certain other minds, which neither astonishes me nor strains my belief. I see clearly enough the moves those great souls make to lift themselves to such a pitch, and I admire their grandeur; I would gladly imitate the flights I think the bravest, and although I lack the wings, my judgment can at least follow along. The other example Bodin holds up as "incredible and wholly fabulous" in Plutarch is that "Agesilaus was fined by the Ephori for having engrossed the hearts and affections of his citizens to himself alone." Here I see no sign of falsity at all. Plutarch is speaking of things that must have been better known to him than to us; and it was no new thing in Greece for men to be punished and exiled for being too popular — witness the ostracism and petalism.

There is in this same passage another charge against Plutarch I cannot stomach, where Bodin says that Plutarch sincerely paralleled Romans with Romans and Greeks with Greeks, but not Romans with Greeks: witness, he says, Demosthenes and Cicero, Cato and Aristides, Sulla and Lysander, Marcellus and Pelopidas, Pompey and Agesilaus — and that he favoured the Greeks by giving them such unequal partners. This is really to attack what is best in Plutarch and most worth praising; for in his Parallels (which is the most admirable part of all his work, and the one with which, I think, he was himself most pleased) the fidelity and sincerity of his judgments equal their depth and weight. He is a philosopher who teaches us virtue. Let us see whether we can defend him from this charge of falsity and bias. All I can imagine giving rise to the censure is the great and shining glamour of the Roman names we have in our minds: it does not seem likely to us that Demosthenes could rival the glory of a consul, proconsul, and praetor of that great Republic. But if you consider the truth of the thing, and the men in themselves — which is Plutarch's chief aim — and weigh their characters, their natures, and their parts rather than their fortunes, I think (contrary to Bodin) that Cicero and the elder Cato fall far short of the men they are compared with. For Bodin's purpose I would sooner have picked the younger Cato paired with Phocion: in that couple there would have been a more plausible inequality, in the Roman's favour. As for Marcellus, Sulla, and Pompey, I see well enough that their war-exploits are greater and more full of pomp and glory than those of the Greeks Plutarch matches them with; but the bravest and most virtuous actions, in war as elsewhere, are not always the most renowned. I often see the names of captains darkened by the brilliance of others of less merit — witness Labienus, Ventidius, Telesinus, and a few more. And to take it that way: if I had to complain on the Greek side, could I not say that Camillus was much less comparable to Themistocles, the Gracchi to Agis and Cleomenes, and Numa to Lycurgus? But it is folly to judge in one glance things that have so many faces. When Plutarch compares them, he does not for all that make them equal — and who could more learnedly and honestly have marked their distinctions? Does he set the victories, the feats of arms, the strength of the armies Pompey commanded, and his triumphs against those of Agesilaus? "I do not believe," he says, "that Xenophon himself, were he alive, with full leave to write whatever he pleased in Agesilaus' favour, would dare put them in the comparison." Does he speak of paralleling Lysander to Sulla? "There is," he says, "no comparison, either in the number of victories or in the risks of battles, for Lysander only won two naval battles." This is not to belittle the Romans: simply by naming them alongside the Greeks he can have done them no harm, whatever the gap between them — and Plutarch does not set them flatly opposite each other. There is no overall verdict; he only compares the pieces and circumstances one by one and gives each a separate judgment. So if anyone wants to convict him of partiality he ought to point to one of those particular judgments, or to say in general that he was wrong to match a given Greek with a given Roman when there were others better suited to pair him with.
